items.question: How do I calculate the future value of annuity contributions?
items.answer: Grow the starting balance and each contribution for the time it is invested. With monthly end deposits C, monthly equivalent rate j and N months, the deposit portion is C × ((1+j)^N − 1)/j; add growth on initial principal and separately timed annual deposits. At zero return, simply add the starting amount and contributions.

items.question: Can I combine monthly and annual deposits and change their timing?
items.answer: Yes. Both additions are included. Beginning timing places monthly deposits at month start and annual deposits at the start of each saving year; End timing places them at the corresponding ends. At a positive return, earlier contributions earn longer. A partial final year receives an annual deposit only if its scheduled deposit date is reached.

items.question: Is the annuity growth rate a guaranteed insurance return?
items.answer: No. The entered rate is a constant projection assumption. Actual annuity contracts can have explicit fees, implicit costs, caps and withdrawal restrictions. This page does not price those terms or an insurer’s guarantees. Review the specific contract and use a consistent rate assumption; a positive projected balance is not a recommendation to buy an annuity.

items.question: Is annuity accumulation the same as monthly retirement income?
items.answer: No. Accumulation estimates a future balance while you are adding money. Annuity Payout estimates period-end withdrawals from an existing balance under a constant return and chosen term or payment. Lifetime insurance payments can depend on contract guarantees and life-contingent pricing that neither projection supplies.

items.question: Does this include annuity taxes and surrender charges?
items.answer: No. It projects contributions and growth without calculating tax treatment, surrender charges, death benefits or optional riders. items.question: How is a fixed annuity payout calculated in this model?
items.answer: Choose Fix Length and enter the balance, effective annual return, payout frequency and term. For complete periods, payment = principal × j / (1 − (1+j)^−N), where j is the equivalent payout-period rate. At zero return, divide principal by the number of periods. The schedule separates investment earnings from principal being returned.

items.answer: No. Annualized cash paid divided by principal is a payout ratio, and it can include your own principal. It is not the rate earned on the investment. items.question: Why does payout frequency change the result?
items.answer: Monthly, quarterly and annual payments arrive at different times. The model converts the same effective annual return to the corresponding period rate, with payments at period end. Frequency affects how long money remains invested. In Fix Length a partial final period can produce a different final payout, so inspect the schedule rather than multiplying a rounded regular payment by a fractional count.

items.answer: No. Obtain the monthly benefit and any lump-sum or survivor quotes from your plan administrator. items.answer: The displayed Undiscounted break-even years is entered lump sum divided by twelve times the initial monthly pension. items.question: How should I set pension COLA and the discount rate?
items.answer: Use the actual plan terms for COLA and a consistent nominal annual discount assumption. A real discount rate combined with nominal COLA can count inflation inconsistently. Test several plausible assumptions and keep them the same across options.

social-security.summary: Compare Social Security retirement claiming ages using an entered benefit estimate, assumed COLA, discount rate and lifespan. social-security.scope: US retirement-benefit comparison, not a calculation from lifetime earnings. Compare mode takes each nominal claim-date quote as entered, with COLA only after that option starts. Monthly end benefits and anniversary COLAs simplify actual SSA calendars, rounding and credit posting. Earnings-test withholding, benefit taxation, Medicare deductions and spousal/survivor coordination are excluded.
